lesson.title: Greetings and manners
lesson.body:
Hola means hello and gracias means thank you. Add por favor and you are already polite.

Use buenos días until noon and buenas tardes after.

¿Qué tal? is a friendly "how are you?" and mucho gusto means "nice to meet you".

Try it: say hello, please and thank you out loud in Spanish five times today.

lesson.title: Repotting with confidence
lesson.body:
Repot when roots circle the pot or poke out of the bottom, ideally in spring.

Choose a pot only one size up with drainage holes.

Loosen circling roots gently with your fingers and set the plant at the same depth it grew before.

Try it: tip one plant out of its pot and look at the roots. White and firm is healthy; brown and mushy means it is staying too wet.

lesson.title: Watering rhythm
lesson.body:
Check the soil with a finger. If the top inch is dry, water thoroughly; if not, wait.

Overwatering kills far more plants than forgetting.

Water at the base until it runs out of the drainage holes, then empty the saucer so roots never sit in water.

Try it: do the finger test on every plant today and only water the ones that are dry an inch down.

lesson.title: Layering light to dark
lesson.body:
Always paint the lightest tones first. Once a layer dries completely, glaze a darker one on top.

Watercolour is transparent, so you cannot paint white back over dark. Plan your highlights by leaving paper bare.

Test dryness with the back of your hand: if the paper feels cool, it is still damp.

Try it: paint a simple apple in three layers, waiting for each one to dry fully.

lesson.title: Wet-on-wet washes
lesson.body:
Wet the paper first, then touch in colour and watch it bloom. This is how you get soft skies and dreamy backgrounds.

Tilt the paper gently to guide the pigment. Let happy accidents happen.

Too much water makes blooms you cannot control; the paper should shine, not puddle.

Try it: paint three small skies wet-on-wet, each with a different amount of water on the paper.

lesson.title: Meet your paints
lesson.body:
Watercolour comes in pans or tubes. Pans are great for beginners: just add a drop of water and the pigment wakes up.

Start with three colours: a warm and a cool of each primary. You can mix almost anything from them.

Swatch every colour on a strip of paper and label it. You will learn how strong each pigment is.

Try it: make a swatch card with your three primaries and one mix between each pair.

lesson.title: Functions you can reuse
lesson.body:
A function packages steps under a name. Define it once with def, then call it whenever you need it.

Functions can take inputs and give back a result with return.

def greet(name): return "Hi " + name gives you a reusable greeting. greet("Sam") hands back "Hi Sam".

Try it: write a function that takes a price and returns it with 20% added.

lesson.title: Loops that repeat
lesson.body:
A for loop runs the same steps for each item in a list. Instead of ten print lines, write one loop.

Python uses indentation to know what is inside the loop.

for fruit in ["apple", "pear", "plum"]: print(fruit) prints each fruit on its own line.

Try it: write a loop that prints the numbers 1 to 5, each followed by the word "hop".

lesson.title: Variables are labelled boxes
lesson.body:
A variable is a name that points at a value. Write age = 12 and Python remembers it for you.

Names should say what is inside: price is better than p.

You can change what a variable holds at any time: write age = 13 next year and the old value is gone.

Try it: create variables for your name, your favourite number and a city, then print a sentence that uses all three.

lesson.title: Scoring and baking
lesson.body:
Score the loaf with a sharp blade so it can expand. Bake in a very hot, lidded pot for steam.

Remove the lid for the last 15 minutes to get a deep golden crust.

Let the loaf cool for at least an hour before slicing. The crumb is still setting inside.

Try it: practise scoring a single confident line at a shallow angle on your next loaf.

lesson.title: Stretch and fold
lesson.body:
Instead of heavy kneading, wet your hands and gently stretch the dough then fold it over itself every 30 minutes.

This builds strength and gives an open, airy crumb.

Four sets of folds over two hours is plenty. The dough should go from shaggy to smooth and springy.

Try it: do one stretch and fold, wait 30 minutes and notice how much smoother the dough feels.

lesson.title: Feeding your starter
lesson.body:
Your starter is a living mix of flour and water. Feed it equal weights daily and it will bubble up within hours.

A ripe starter doubles in size and smells pleasantly sour.

Keep it at room temperature and use a jar with straight sides so you can mark the level with a rubber band.

Try it: feed your starter, mark the level, and check how long it takes to double.

lesson.title: Editing with a light touch
lesson.body:
Nudge exposure, lift shadows and add a touch of warmth. Stop before it looks edited.

Compare with the original often to keep your edit honest.

Crop and straighten first, then adjust light, then colour. Small steps in that order keep edits natural.

Try it: edit one photo three times with different moods, then pick the version that feels most like the moment.

lesson.title: Composition: thirds and lines
lesson.body:
Turn on your grid. Put the subject on an intersection instead of the centre.

Leading lines like roads or fences pull the eye through the frame.

Leave space in front of a moving subject so it has somewhere to go in the frame.

Try it: take five photos on your walk today, each using a leading line toward the subject.

lesson.title: Chasing golden hour
lesson.body:
The hour after sunrise and before sunset gives warm, soft light that flatters everything.

Place your subject so the light grazes it from the side for gentle depth.

Cloudy days act like a giant softbox, so do not put your phone away when the sun hides.

Try it: photograph the same object at noon and again an hour before sunset, then compare the two.

lesson.title: Asking directions
lesson.body:
Dónde está... means where is. ¿Dónde está la estación?

Listen for derecha (right), izquierda (left) and todo recto (straight on).

Add perdone (excuse me) before your question and people will be happy to help.

Try it: pick three places near you and practise asking where each one is.

lesson.title: Ordering food
lesson.body:
Say Quisiera and the dish you want. Quisiera una paella, por favor.

La cuenta, por favor asks for the bill.

Para mí... means "for me..." and is a relaxed way to order: para mí, el pollo.

Try it: order your next meal at home in Spanish, out loud, including asking for the bill.

lesson.title: Compound interest
lesson.body:
Interest earns interest. Money left alone grows faster every year.

The earlier you start, the more time does the heavy lifting.

At 6% a year, money roughly doubles every 12 years. That is the rule of 72: divide 72 by the rate.

Try it: use the rule of 72 to work out how long 1,000 euros takes to double at 4%, 6% and 8%.

lesson.title: Your emergency fund
lesson.body:
Aim to save three to six months of essential expenses in an easy-access account.

Start tiny: even a small automatic transfer builds the habit.

Keep it separate from your everyday account so it is easy to reach in a crisis but not tempting on a Friday night.

Try it: set up a small automatic transfer for the day after payday, even if it is only 10 euros.

lesson.title: The 50/30/20 budget
lesson.body:
Split take-home pay: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt repayment.

It is a starting point, not a rule. Adjust it to your life.

Needs are bills you must pay: rent, groceries, transport. Wants are everything that makes life nicer but could pause.

Try it: list last month's spending in three columns and see how close you are to 50/30/20.

lesson.title: Light and placement
lesson.body:
Most houseplants love bright, indirect light. A spot near an east or north window is a safe bet.

Pale, leggy growth means a plant is reaching for more light.

Rotate pots a quarter turn each week so every side gets its share and the plant grows straight.

Try it: walk around your home at noon and note which windows get direct sun. Move one plant that looks stretched closer to the light.

lesson.title: Test with five people
lesson.body:
Five test users uncover most usability problems. Give them a task and stay quiet.

Watch where they hesitate. That is where your design needs work.

Write the task as a goal, not instructions: "find a gift under 20 euros", not "click Shop".

Try it: run a five-minute test with one person on any app you use. Note every place they pause for more than a second.

lesson.title: Sketch before pixels
lesson.body:
Paper is fast and cheap. Sketch ten rough ideas before opening any design tool.

Rough sketches invite honest feedback because nobody is attached yet.

Set a timer for eight minutes and sketch one idea per minute. Quantity first, judgement later.

Try it: sketch eight versions of a simple sign-up screen, then circle the two you would test.

lesson.title: What users really want
lesson.body:
People rarely want your product; they want a job done. Ask about the last time they tried.

Listen for frustrations and workarounds, not feature requests.

Ask open questions like "walk me through the last time you did this" and let silences run a little long.

Try it: interview one friend about the last time they booked a trip. Write down three frustrations they mention.

quiz_question.prompt: Which paints are best for beginners starting out?
quiz_question.explanation: Pans are simple, tidy and need just a drop of water.

quiz_question.prompt: How many colours do you need to start mixing?
quiz_question.explanation: Warm and cool primaries mix almost anything.

quiz_question.prompt: In wet-on-wet, what do you do first?
quiz_question.explanation: A wet surface lets colour bloom and blend.

quiz_question.prompt: Which tones go down first?
quiz_question.explanation: Watercolour is transparent, so light comes first.

quiz_question.prompt: What does age = 12 do in Python?
quiz_question.explanation: Assignment stores a value under a name.

quiz_question.prompt: What marks the code inside a Python loop?
quiz_question.explanation: Python uses indentation to group code.

quiz_question.prompt: Which keyword gives a result back from a function?
quiz_question.explanation: return hands a value back to the caller.

quiz_question.prompt: A ripe starter usually...
quiz_question.explanation: Doubling shows lots of active yeast.

quiz_question.prompt: Why stretch and fold instead of kneading?
quiz_question.explanation: Gentle folds build gluten and an open crumb.

quiz_question.prompt: Why bake in a lidded pot?
quiz_question.explanation: Steam keeps the crust soft so the loaf can rise.

quiz_question.prompt: When is golden hour?
quiz_question.option_c: Just after sunrise and before sunset
quiz_question.explanation: Low sun means warm, soft light.

quiz_question.prompt: Where might you place your subject by the rule of thirds?
quiz_question.explanation: Intersections feel balanced and dynamic.

quiz_question.prompt: What is a good editing approach?
quiz_question.explanation: Light edits keep photos natural.

quiz_question.prompt: What does gracias mean?
quiz_question.explanation: Gracias = thank you.

quiz_question.prompt: How do you ask for the bill?
quiz_question.explanation: La cuenta is the bill.

quiz_question.prompt: What does derecha mean?
quiz_question.explanation: Derecha = right.

quiz_question.prompt: In 50/30/20, what is the 20% for?
quiz_question.explanation: 20% goes to your future self.

quiz_question.prompt: How big should an emergency fund be?
quiz_question.explanation: It covers essentials if income stops.

quiz_question.prompt: Compound interest means...
quiz_question.option_b: Interest only on the start sum
quiz_question.explanation: Growth builds on past growth.

quiz_question.prompt: What should you listen for in interviews?
quiz_question.explanation: Pain points reveal real needs.

quiz_question.prompt: Why sketch on paper first?
quiz_question.explanation: Low effort keeps ideas flexible.

quiz_question.prompt: How many users find most usability issues?
quiz_question.explanation: Five is usually enough to spot patterns.

quiz_question.prompt: Pale, leggy growth means a plant needs...
quiz_question.explanation: It is stretching toward light.

quiz_question.prompt: When should you water?
quiz_question.option_d: When the top inch is dry
quiz_question.explanation: Check the soil first.

quiz_question.prompt: How much bigger should the new pot be?
quiz_question.explanation: Too much soil stays wet and rots roots.
